focus: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model

items.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
items.source: Rafailov, Sharma, Mitchell, Ermon, Manning, Finn (Stanford); NeurIPS 2023
items.why: DPO replaced PPO-based RLHF as the default preference-tuning recipe in much of open-source post-training. The derivation is a clean piece of applied math (Bradley-Terry plus a KL-constrained optimum with a closed form), exactly the kind of reasoning that lets you understand alignment methods instead of just calling a trainer.
items.summary:
Standard RLHF fits a reward model on preference pairs using the Bradley-Terry model, where the probability that y1 beats y2 depends only on the reward difference through a sigmoid. It then maximizes expected reward minus beta times the KL divergence to a reference policy, usually with PPO, which needs sampling from the policy, a baseline, and a lot of tuning.

The key observation: the KL-regularized objective has a closed-form optimum, pi*(y|x) proportional to pi_ref(y|x) * exp(r(x,y)/beta). Rearranging gives the reward as beta times the log-ratio of policy to reference, plus beta times log Z(x), where Z is an intractable partition function depending only on x. Because Bradley-Terry only uses reward differences between two completions of the same prompt, the log Z term cancels. The preference probability can therefore be written purely in terms of the policy and the reference model.

That turns reward-model fitting plus RL into a single binary cross-entropy loss over (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples: maximize the sigmoid of beta times the difference in log-ratios between chosen and rejected. The policy itself is the only trained network, and its implicit reward is beta times log(pi_theta/pi_ref). The gradient raises the likelihood of the chosen completion and lowers the rejected one, weighted by how wrongly the implicit reward currently ranks the pair, which is what stops the objective from degenerating into plain unlikelihood training. Beta controls how far the policy may drift from the reference; larger beta stays closer.

The paper reports a better reward-vs-KL frontier than PPO on controlled sentiment generation, and competitive or better GPT-4-judged win rates on TL;DR summarization and Anthropic-HH dialogue, with more robustness to sampling temperature. Experiments go up to about 6B parameters, so treat the scaling claims with care. Note the limits: it is offline on a fixed preference set, and it only sees likelihoods of sequences, so it can reduce the probability of both chosen and rejected completions in practice.
items.exercise: In Python with PyTorch and a small model (e.g. a ~100M-parameter GPT-2 style checkpoint), implement the DPO loss by hand: compute summed token log-probs for chosen and rejected under the policy and a frozen reference copy, apply -log sigmoid(beta * (delta_chosen - delta_rejected)), and train on a small public preference set for a few hundred steps. Log the implicit reward margin and the log-prob of chosen completions over time, and check whether chosen log-probs drop. Then sweep beta in {0.05, 0.1, 0.5} and compare KL to the reference.

items.title: CRDTs: Consistency without concurrency control
items.source: Letia, Preguica, Shapiro (INRIA Research Report RR-6956, 2009)
items.why: This is where the term CRDT was introduced. It shows the real engineering cost of coordination-free convergence: identifier design, tombstones, and the fact that garbage collection quietly brings consensus back. Essential background for local-first software, collaborative editing, and multi-region replicated state.
items.summary:
The premise is that if every concurrent operation on a data type commutes, and replicas apply all operations in causal order, replicas converge without locks, consensus, or last-writer-wins style data loss. The authors build a non-trivial existence proof: Treedoc, a shared text buffer.

For an ordered sequence you need identifiers for each atom that are unique, stable for the lifetime of the document, totally ordered, and dense, so a new identifier can always be allocated between any two existing ones. Treedoc uses paths in a binary tree, ordered by in-order traversal. Concurrent inserts that choose the same position are disambiguated by mini-nodes tagged with a site identifier. Insert and delete operations take a fresh ID and are idempotent, so duplicate delivery is harmless, and operations on different IDs commute.

Deletes leave tombstones, because the position must remain addressable for concurrent operations. Without cleanup, the paper reports that the large majority of nodes in a heavily edited Wikipedia page are tombstones, and path identifiers grow. The fix is a flatten operation that rebuilds the tree as a compact array and drops tombstones. Flatten does not commute with updates, so it uses an update-wins rule and needs a commit protocol (two-phase or Paxos commit) among sites. The design splits replicas into a small well-connected core that runs the commits and a nebula of loosely connected sites that catch up by mapping old identifiers to new ones.

The takeaway is architectural: the hot path (edits) is coordination-free, while metadata cleanup is pushed off the critical path to a rare consensus step. The paper's performance numbers come from one 2009 trace, so use them for intuition rather than as benchmarks.
items.exercise: Implement a minimal sequence CRDT in C# or Python. Simplest route: an RGA or Logoot-style list where each element has a unique, totally ordered ID (e.g. a list of (digit, siteId) pairs, allocating between neighbors) plus a tombstone flag. Simulate 3 replicas applying random concurrent inserts and deletes with shuffled delivery (respecting causality), and assert all replicas converge to the same string. Then measure tombstone count and average ID length after 10,000 random edits and write a naive compaction.

items.title: RocksDB Tuning Guide
items.why: RocksDB underlies a huge amount of infrastructure (Kafka Streams state stores, CockroachDB, TiKV, Flink state). Understanding the read, write and space amplification trade-off is the practical way to reason about LSM engines, and it carries over to Cassandra, ScyllaDB and any LSM-based store.
items.summary:
The guide frames everything through three amplifications. Write amplification is bytes written to storage divided by bytes written by the application. Read amplification is physical reads per query. Space amplification is on-disk size divided by logical data size. You cannot minimize all three; compaction style and parameters pick a point in the trade-off.

Writes go to an active memtable (a skiplist by default). When it reaches write_buffer_size it becomes immutable and is flushed to an L0 SST file. max_write_buffer_number bounds how many memtables can exist; if flushing falls behind, writes stall. L0 files may overlap in key range, and L0 to L1 compaction triggers on file count. Slowdown and stop thresholds on L0 file count (and pending compaction bytes) are the mechanism behind write stalls, which show up as latency cliffs rather than gradual degradation.

Leveled compaction, the default, keeps each level above L0 non-overlapping and about 10x bigger than the previous one. A point lookup checks at most one file per level beyond L0, but each byte may be rewritten roughly once per level crossing, which is why write amplification of tens is normal. Space amplification stays low (about 1.1x in the guide's worked example). Universal compaction merges sorted runs by size ratio, giving lower write amplification at the cost of higher read and space amplification, and it can temporarily need up to double the space.

On the read side, bloom filters (default 10 bits per key, about 1 percent false positives) skip files that cannot contain a key, but do nothing for range scans, where read cost is roughly the L0 file count plus the number of non-empty levels. The block cache holds uncompressed blocks, while the OS page cache holds compressed ones, so both matter. The guide also warns that heavy tuning on SSDs tends to regress when workload or hardware shifts, so tune only against a measured problem. Note this is a tuning guide, not a full internals reference; the linked Compaction and Write-Stalls pages go deeper.
items.exercise: Use RocksDB (python-rocksdb or RocksDbSharp, or db_bench) and run a fillrandom workload with 50M-100M small keys under leveled vs universal compaction. Record write amplification from rocksdb.stats, p99 write latency, stall counts, and final disk size. Then run readrandom with and without bloom filters and compare read throughput. Write a one-page table of the three amplifications for each configuration.

items.title: FHIR Search (HL7 FHIR Specification)
items.why: Search semantics are where FHIR servers get hard: token systems and codes, hierarchical terminology modifiers, chaining and includes. Reading the spec as a storage and indexing problem is the best way to judge whether a FHIR facade over SQL, a document store or a search engine will hold up.
items.summary:
FHIR search is defined over typed search parameters: number, date, string, token, reference, composite, quantity, uri and special. Each type has its own matching rules. A token matches a system plus code pair, a date matches by precision-aware ranges, a string is case- and accent-insensitive prefix match by default, and a quantity involves value, units and system. Prefixes such as gt, lt, ge, le, sa, eb and ap apply to number, date and quantity.

Modifiers change semantics: exact and contains for strings, missing for presence, not for tokens, in and not-in for ValueSet membership, above and below for hierarchies, and a type modifier to restrict reference targets. Servers must reject unsupported modifiers with an error rather than silently ignoring them. Combination logic is simple: separate parameters are ANDed and comma-separated values within one parameter are ORed.

Results come back as a Bundle of type searchset, with entries marked match, include or outcome. _include follows references forward and _revinclude backward from matches, with :iterate repeating the process and the server choosing depth limits, and with wildcard forms advertised via the CapabilityStatement. Chaining and reverse chaining via _has express joins across resource types. Paging uses _count and link relations; _total is a hint (none, estimate or accurate), and _count=0 returns only the total. Sorting is by comma-separated parameters with a leading minus for descending.

The indexing implications are the interesting part: token search needs separate system and code storage and, for :below, :above and :in, terminology closure tables; dates need stored range bounds with precision; reference chains and includes imply joins; :missing and :not need presence indexes. The spec does not mandate an implementation and suggests full-text engines for text search. Chaining and modifier details are long, so read the relevant sections directly when implementing.
items.exercise: Design and build a tiny FHIR-style search layer over Postgres in C# or Python for Patient and Observation. Store resources as JSONB plus an extracted search-index table (resource_id, param, system, code, value, date_low, date_high). Implement token search with system|code, date with eq/gt/lt prefixes using range overlap, chaining (Observation?subject:Patient.name=...) and _include. Check EXPLAIN output and add the indexes that make each query avoid sequential scans.
